blocks.x: The easiest way to say “I understand” in Japanese is わかります (wakarimasu, meaning “to understand”), but it doesn’t always capture every nuance. Similar to English, the phrases “I know,” “I understand,” and “I comprehend” carry subtly different meanings despite their similarity. In Japanese, this complexity runs even deeper, since certain phrases can sound more polite or more casual depending on the context.
So let’s go over some common expressions for saying “I understand,” and when you would and wouldn’t use 分かります (wakarimasu).
1. わかります (Wakarimasu) and When Not to Use It
わかります (wakarimasu) directly translates to “to understand” or “to comprehend” in a general sense. For example, if you are saying that you understand English, you could say:
Example:

英語がわかります。
Eigo ga wakarimasu.
I understand English
When Not to Use わかります (Wakarimasu)

わかります describes general comprehension, not how well you understand a situation, new information, or a request. Using わかります in this context would sound awkward and unnatural, even though the English equivalent “I understand” would work in these scenarios.

Instead, use the past tense: わかりました (wakarimashita). It can be used to express your understanding in a wide variety of contexts; it serves as an excellent response to someone, such as public or service staff, who are explaining something to you.
Example:

スタッフ：新宿行きの電車は階段を上がって右です。
Sutaffu: Shinjuku yuki no densha wa kaidan o agatte migi desu.
Staff: The train to Shinjuku is up the stairs, on the right.

あなた：わかりました！ありがとうございます！
Anata: Wakarimashita! Arigatou gozaimasu!
You: Understood! Thank you so much!

You can also use it to respond enthusiastically to commands from a colleague or senpai, similar to saying “understood” or “got it!” Beyond work, わかりました is quite versatile, commonly used in daily life. You can use it to show your understanding of something, like a decision somebody made, how something came to be, and more. But it’s far from the only way to say “I understand” in Japanese.
Other Ways to Say “I Understand” in Japanese
So what are some other ways to say “I understand” beyond わかります or わかりました? Some phrases fit better in formal or casual contexts and have different uses that work better in different situations.
It’s also useful to know how to say “I don’t understand,” so read our blog to find out everything you need to know: Wakaranai: 8 Ways to Say “I Don’t Understand” in Japanese
2. 承知致しました (Shouchi Itashimashita)

承知致しました (Shouchi Itashimashita) is a great Japanese business phrase you can use to express “I understand” in a professional setting. It’s an effective and polite response to a senior making a request or teaching you something new.

It conveys humility and respect to the person you’re speaking to. The phrase 致しました is actually the keigo humble form of します, which is used whenever you would like to lower your position in favor of the listener. So with keigo built into this expression, it’s perfect to use with your boss or anyone else deserving of high respect!
Example:

上司：この会議で前期の数字を報告してもらえますか？
Joushi: kono kaigi ni zenki no suuji o hokoku shite moraemaska?
Boss: Can you report last quarter’s numbers in the meeting?

あなた：承知致しました！
Anata: Shouchi itashimashita!
You: Understood!
3. かしこまりました (Kashikomarimashita)

Another useful expression you will often use in Japanese business settings is かしこまりました (Kashikomarimashita), which means something close to “understood!”, “got it!”, or “will do!” It’s similar to わかりました (wakarimashita), but it’s even more appropriate in business settings.
Just like 承知致しました (shouchiitashimashita), this phrase is great for responding to your boss or other colleagues.

先輩：新しいデザインを制作してもらえますか？
Senpai: Atarashii dezain o seisaku shite moraemasuka?
Senpai: Can you please create a new design?

あなた：はい、かしこまりました！
Anata: Hai, kashikomarimashita!
You: Yes, understood!
4. 了解です (Ryoukai Desu)

了解です (ryoukai desu) means something like “roger!” or “got it!” but it works very similarly to わかりました (wakarishimashita). It’s a great enthusiastic response to a request, favor, or agreement to do something. You can use it among colleagues at work or even with friends when deciding to meet up somewhere. So, this phrase works in both casual and formal contexts.
In casual settings, you drop です (desu), so all you have to say is 了解 (ryoukai). So, use 了解 next time someone asks you to do something!
Example:

友達：今晩7時に渋谷駅で待ち合わせしよう。
Tomodachi: Konban shichiji ni Shibuya eki de machiawase shiyou.
Friend: Let’s meet at Shibuya station at 7 pm tonight.

あなた：了解です！
Anata: Ryoukai desu!
You: Got it!
5. りー
りー is actually a shortened, casual slang form of 了解, which means “roger!” or “got it!” It comes from the first character of 了解, written in hiragana as りょうかい.
りょうかい → り/りー

It shares the same meaning as 了解, but it’s used in a much more casual context, like texting between friends. It’s Gen Z slang that likely evolved from texting on social media apps like LINE. It is still mostly used on social media, but it has made its way to real-life conversation as well.
Example:

友達：渋谷のハチ公銅像に会おう！
Tomodachi: shibuya no hachiko douzou ni aou!
Friend: Let’s meet at the Hachiko statue!

あなた：りー！
Anata: rii!
You: Got it!
6. わかった (Wakatta)

わかった (wakatta) is the plain, casual past-tense form of わかる (wakaru), and it’s what you’ll hear most often among friends or close coworkers instead of the polite わかりました. Dropping the ます form makes it sound relaxed and natural, perfect for everyday conversations where formality isn’t needed.
Example:

友達：今日は忙しいから、先に帰ってもいい？
Tomodachi: Kyou wa isogashii kara, saki ni kaettemo ii?
Friend: I’m busy today; is it okay if I head home first?

あなた：わかった、また明日ね！
Anata: Wakatta, mata ashita ne!
You: Got it, see you tomorrow!

Because it’s plain form, save わかった for people you’re close to, like friends, family, or coworkers on equal footing with you. Stick to the polite forms with anyone above you or anyone you don’t know well.
7. OKです

OKです (OK desu) is a casual, borrowed-from-English loanword meaning “okay” or “got it” in Japanese. It doesn’t carry the same nuance of comprehension as わかります; it’s more of a quick, breezy way to agree to something or confirm you’ve received a message.
Example:

友達：チケット２枚予約しておいたんだけど、よかった？
Tomodachi: Chiketto nimai shite oitandakedo, yokatta?
Friend: I already booked two tickets, is that okay?

あなた：OKです、ありがとう！
Anata: OK desu, arigatou!
You: Okay, thanks!
OKです works as a great casual response to a friend asking a question for confirmation, for example, when they are asking something like よかった？ (yokkata), or “is that okay?”
8. ご存知です

ご存知です (gozonji desu) actually means “you understand,” not “I understand,” since you would only use it for the person you’re talking to. ご存知 is the honorific keigo form of わかる (wakaru), so you would never use it to describe your own understanding. You usually use it to ask whether the listener understands or knows something.
This phrase is very respectful and raises the listener above your own status. It’s typically used when you are talking to your boss, a senior colleague, or a client/customer.
Example:

山田さんが本日お休みであることは、ご存知でしょうか？
Yamadasan ga honjitsu oyasumi de arukoto ha gozonji deshouka?
Did you know that Yamada-san is off today?
9. 理解する (Rikai Suru)

理解する (rikai suru) also means “I understood” or “I comprehend,” but it carries a slightly different nuance where you’ve grasped something like a concept, an explanation, or someone’s feelings and circumstances. However, in Japanese conversation, it is rarely used as a single affirmative statement.
Depending on the context, you might use it in potential form, such as 理解できる (rikai dekiru), meaning “I can understand/comprehend. But it is most frequently used when making a request to someone else.
For instance, a common expression you might hear is ご理解のほどよろしくお願いいたします (Go-rikai no hodo yoroshiku onegai itashimasu), meaning “We ask for your understanding.”
Example:

現在、多くのお問い合わせをいただいているため、ご返信まで3～5営業日ほどお時間を頂戴しております。恐れ入りますが、ご理解の程よろしくお願いいたします。
Genzai ooku no otoiawase o itadaite iru tame, go henshin made 3~5 eigyoubi hodo ojikan o choudai shite orimasu. Osore irimasu ga, gokirai no hodo yoroshiku onegai itashimasu.
Recently, due to the high volume of inquiries, it may take around 3 to 5 business days to respond. We deeply appreciate your kind understanding.
10. なるほど (Naruhodo)

なるほど (naruhodo) translates closer to “I see” or “that makes sense,” and it’s a great phrase to use when new information clicks for you mid-conversation. Unlike わかりました, which confirms you’ll act on something, なるほど shows that you followed someone’s explanation or reasoning.
Example:

友達：このアプリ、住所を入力しなくても注文できるんだよ。
Tomodachi: Kono apuri, juusho o nyuuryoku shinakutemo chuumon dekirunda yo.
Friend: With this app, you can order without even entering your address.

あなた：なるほど、便利だね！
Anata: Naruhodo, benri da ne!
You: I see, that’s convenient!

Because なるほど is casual and conversational, it fits best in everyday chats with friends or family. Just be careful using it with superiors, since it can come across as slightly condescending, as if you’re evaluating what they said rather than simply acknowledging it.
Conclusion: There Are Many Ways to Say “I Understand” in Japanese

There are a plethora of ways to say “I understand” in Japanese, but generally you can use the phrase わかりました (wakarimashita) or its casual counterpart 分かった (wakatta) to express your understanding in most situations!

But you will definitely hear and use the other phrases on this list, which are commonly used in different circumstances such as work or social media. Try to remember a few from this list and start using them in your daily life!
